turns.user: is it normal for a landlord to keep the whole deposit if i leave before the lease ends? im in ontario, lease is up in march but we have to move in jan bc of a job thing
turns.assistant:
Ending a lease early isn't the same as losing the deposit, so those are two separate questions. In Ontario the deposit is usually last month's rent, and the landlord can only keep it for unpaid rent or damage, or if you owe money under the lease. Breaking the lease early doesn't by itself mean they get to keep it.

What you can actually be on the hook for is the rent for the rest of the term, since you're still bound to the lease until it ends or someone else takes over. The landlord also has a duty to try to re-rent the unit, so you shouldn't be liable for the whole remaining amount if they could reasonably fill it.

If you give proper written notice, check the lease for any early termination clause before you assume the worst.

turns.user: ok but if they find someone new in dec do i still owe the rest
turns.assistant:
Usually not for the period after the new tenant starts paying. If a new tenant moves in in December and the rent is covered from that date, your liability for the remaining months should stop there, as long as the landlord was actively trying to find someone.

You'd still owe rent from when you move out until the new tenant's start date, plus any advertising or cleaning costs that are reasonable. Keep copies of any listings, messages or showing dates you have, because if it ends up in a dispute those are what show the landlord was trying to re-rent.

turns.user: and the last month deposit, can they use that for the new tenant or does it stay with them
turns.assistant:
It stays with them and it's held against the last month of the tenancy. They can't roll it over to the new tenant, since the new tenant pays their own deposit to the landlord.

When you move out, if the unit is in good shape and you've paid everything, they should return it to you, normally with interest, within a reasonable time after you leave. If you want to avoid a fight later, do a move-out walkthrough with them, take dated photos, and get the keys back in writing.

turns.user: postgres q. pulling the latest row per user from an events table. is it better to use row_number() window fn, DISTINCT ON, or a correlated subquery with max(ts)? ~200m rows, there's an index on (user_id, ts)
turns.assistant:
For Postgres specifically, DISTINCT ON is usually the cleanest and often the fastest here.

- DISTINCT ON (user_id) with ORDER BY user_id, ts DESC is short and reads well. With your index it can walk the index and stop per user.
- row_number() over (partition by user_id order by ts desc) is portable across databases and easy to extend (say, top 3 per user), but it has to compute the window over everything, so it's usually a bit heavier.
- The correlated subquery with max(ts) is the one to avoid at 200m rows unless the planner handles it well for your data. It can work with the index, but it's the least predictable of the three.

If you only need one row per user, go with DISTINCT ON.

trying to get more protein on a budget. broke student, dont really cook. what are some options i can rotate through
turns.assistant:
Some cheap, low-effort options:

- Eggs. Hard boil a batch on Sunday and they keep all week.
- Canned tuna or chickpeas. Tuna is around 20g protein per can, and it works on crackers, in wraps or out of the tin.
- Greek yogurt, especially the big tubs. Good with oats or fruit.
- Cottage cheese. Cheap per gram of protein and fine on toast.
- Lentils or red split lentils. Cook a big pot and use them in soups or rice.
- Chicken thighs, bought in bulk when they're on sale.
- Peanut butter, but count the calories since it adds up fast.

If you rotate between eggs, tuna, yogurt and lentils, you'll hit a decent amount without much planning.

turns.user: why does the normal force equal mg on a flat surface but not on an incline? like what actually changes
turns.assistant:
The normal force is the surface pushing back perpendicular to itself. It doesn't have a fixed value. It's whatever it needs to be so that the net force perpendicular to the surface is zero, because the object isn't accelerating into or away from the surface.

On a flat surface, the only force pushing along the perpendicular direction is gravity. So the normal force has to match it: N = mg.

On an incline, gravity points straight down, but the perpendicular direction is tilted. Only part of gravity pushes into the surface, which is mg cos(theta). The rest, mg sin(theta), pulls the object along the slope. So the normal force becomes N = mg cos(theta), and it gets smaller as the incline gets steeper.

turns.user: so on a 30 degree ramp its like 0.87mg? and the friction is the other part?
turns.assistant:
Yes. cos(30) is about 0.866, so N is about 0.87mg.

The along-slope part is mg sin(30), which is 0.5mg. If the block is sitting still, static friction has to push back up the slope with exactly 0.5mg to balance it. If friction can't provide that much, the block slides, and then you'd use kinetic friction, which is mu_k times N, so about mu_k times 0.87mg.

turns.user: were going to tokyo for 4 nights in april with 2 kids (7 and 10). is kyoto doable as a day trip from tokyo or should we just stay there
turns.assistant:
A day trip is possible. The shinkansen from Tokyo to Kyoto takes about two hours and fifteen minutes on the faster trains, so you could leave around 8 and be back by evening.

With two kids, though, a day trip usually means a lot of time on trains and very little time at the sights. Kyoto has a lot of walking between temples, and kids often run out of steam by early afternoon. Staying one or two nights there tends to be a much more relaxed trip, with the Fushimi Inari shrine and Arashiyama easy to do without rushing.

turns.user: how long is the shinkansen from tokyo to kyoto exactly and is it expensive
turns.assistant:
The fastest trains (Nozomi) run around 2 hours 15 minutes from Tokyo Station to Kyoto. Hikari trains are a bit slower, closer to 2 hours 40 minutes.

For price, a standard one-way reserved seat is roughly 14,000 yen for an adult. Children aged 6 to 11 usually pay half fare, and younger kids under 6 ride free on your lap, though they don't get their own seat. Fares change, so check the JR website or the app before you book. A Japan Rail Pass usually isn't worth it just for this one trip, but it can be if you add more long-distance travel.

turns.user: ok so if we do kyoto for 2 nights do we lose a tokyo day, what's the minimum i need in tokyo
turns.assistant:
With four nights total, two in Kyoto leaves you two in Tokyo. That's workable if you're choosy about what you do, but it's tight with kids, because the first day usually goes to jet lag and getting oriented.

If you can, make it three nights in Tokyo and one in Kyoto, or do two and two and plan a light first day. Tokyo has enough for a couple of days: Ueno Park and the zoo, teamLab, Asakusa, and Odaiba for something indoors if it rains. Pick one main thing per day and you'll be fine.
